dimensions.name: Spec & environment orientation

evidence.note: Probes environment before design: python version, torch, triton 3.0.0, torch.cuda.is_available(), H100 device name — genuine Triton/GPU capability orientation matching the [8] environment clause.

Correctly states the core contract (LayerNorm, five projections, mask application, outgoing einsum contraction) and target shapes before coding; no matmul-vs-transpose confusion — the correct reference built at steps 5-8 confirms the direction was parsed.

The precision failure mode ([10]'s 'fp32 accumulation of K-sum under heavy-tailed inputs') was discovered by repeated bf16 tolerance failures, not anticipated up front; keyword scan shows 'cauchy'/'nomask'/'heavy' never appear in reasoning.
Large-N memory footprint (2.15GB intermediates) and shared-memory tiling limits were discovered mid-implementation rather than flagged during orientation, falling short of the [10] anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent solidly clears [5] — it identifies the core contract (outgoing contraction, mask-at-projection, LN/gate/to_out, fp32, 2e-2 tolerance, hidden_dim=128) and notes the shape ranges before writing — and adds genuine Triton/GPU environment probing that [5] does not require, nudging it toward [8]. But it stops short of [8]/[10]: it never distills an itemized cross-check of the subtle points (nomask==ones equivalence, Cauchy heavy tails as a precision constraint), and the numerical/memory failure modes were learned by trial rather than anticipated. That places the observed level at 6.

dimensions.name: Correctness-first decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Opens with a genuine phase structure: writes a pure-PyTorch reference (step 5), a separate golden ref.py (step 8), and plans 'reference → optimized bmm → Triton kernel'. This is real staged intent and a nominal correctness-first ordering, exceeding the pure-monolith anchor.

Begins chasing bf16/TF32 latency optimizations and writing a fused fast kernel before ever verifying a correct Triton kernel across shapes — correctness and performance become entangled from the start, matching the level-3 'starts optimizing before any shape is verified correct' failure.

Oscillates continuously between correct-but-slow (fp32) and fast-but-inaccurate (bf16/fused) versions, rewriting kernel.py ~20 times with no firm exit criterion per milestone; correctness is only ever spot-checked on tiny shapes, never gated across the domain.

Late game still swinging: step 85 flips allow_tf32 on for speed, steps 104-105 revert bf16 back to fp32 for correctness, and it submits (steps 107-108) with a correct-but-far-over-budget kernel. Never established 'Triton matches reference within 2e-2 on all shapes' as a checkpoint before perf work, and never sequenced the input domain (large N / high dim / Cauchy / mask) deliberately.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds the level-0/3 floor: it built a reference and golden implementation and articulated a reference → Triton → tuning ordering (steps 5-9). But it never used that reference as a real milestone gate — it began bf16/TF32 latency optimization by step 13 before any Triton shape was verified correct, then thrashed for ~60 steps oscillating between correct-slow and fast-inaccurate variants (steps 31-105) with no concrete per-milestone exit criterion and only small-shape spot checks, never sequencing the domain (large N/high dim/Cauchy/mask). This sits between the level-3 'implicit ordering, optimizes before verifying' description and the level-5 'clear phases with a rough notion of done', landing at 4.

dimensions.name: Self-built correctness oracle across the domain

evidence.note: Deliberately wrote a separate pure-PyTorch reference implementation (ref.py) as a golden oracle to check the kernel against — the core of a self-built verification instrument.

Compared kernel to reference using max_diff/violation counts against the correct tolerance formula (atol + rtol*|ref|), reasoning about worst-case error vs the 2e-2 gate — a genuine tolerance-based check.
Only single mention of testing 'with/without mask, different dims'; mask coverage is weakly evidenced and not systematically executed.
grep for 'cauchy' returns zero matches — the heavy-tailed Cauchy distribution (a flagged fragile case) is never included in any correctness check.

Final checks assert correctness on 'multiple small shapes' with max_diff<=0.04 and hand-wave that atol absorbs a few violations, rather than a systematic full-domain sweep or targeted stress on large/Cauchy cases.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built a real independent PyTorch reference oracle and repeatedly checked the kernel against it using the exact rtol=atol=2e-2 tolerance, covering both small and large N (up to 2048) and multiple dims, with explicit worst-case-error reasoning — clearly above anchor 3. But it never once tested the Cauchy distribution (grep=0) and only lightly touched masked cases, so it fails anchor 5's requirement of at least one masked and one Cauchy case, and there is no systematic parameterized sweep. This places it at a 4: a genuine oracle with decent shape/dim coverage but a critical distribution gap and no formal domain sweep.

dimensions.name: Tracking correctness coverage and latency headroom

evidence.note: The same right-tile stride-swap bug is 'found and fixed' repeatedly across the run, and the tl.trans issue is rediscovered several times, with no recognition that it is re-solving an already-solved problem — classic uncaught circular debugging.

Persistent oscillation between bf16-contraction (fast, fails tolerance) and fp32-Triton (correct, too slow) and fused kernels, 'reverting' back and forth many times without ever naming the thrash or committing to a resolution.

Correctness is verified only on tiny/small shapes and treated as 'passes'; Cauchy distribution and large-N correctness never tested, yet the agent declares success — conflating 'passed one small shape' with 'passed' and declaring completion with the domain largely untested.

Latency numbers for the binding N=2048 shape reported inconsistently (45/86/238/52ms) across rewrites; the agent does correctly and repeatedly identify N=2048 as the bottleneck but never establishes a stable per-shape readout over all 10 shapes.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows some usable latency awareness — it reliably identifies N=2048 as the binding worst-case shape and quotes rough per-shape numbers — which lifts it above a pure 0-2. But its correctness tracking conflates a single small-shape pass with domain-wide correctness (never testing Cauchy or large-N), and it repeatedly re-fixes the same stride bug while oscillating between bf16/fp32 approaches without ever detecting or naming the circular debugging, ultimately declaring success with the domain untested. This matches the anchor-3 profile ('vague tracking; conflates passed one shape with passed') with pronounced anchor-0 traits (repeats the same failed fix), landing at a 3.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on numerical & performance failures

evidence.note: Diagnoses that TF32 was disabled and that fp32 bmm (~11ms for N=2048) exceeds budget; correctly reasons about tensor-core TFLOPS and pivots toward bf16/tf32 for the contraction — a genuine evidence-driven design change.
Root-causes a Triton compile/correctness failure to a missing base pointer in tl.load and fixes the specific cause, then re-verifies — level-5-style targeted fix.

Repeated stride-order debugging on the transposed right tile: makes several competing offset hypotheses (some wrong), reverting layout back and forth. Real diagnosis but noticeably thrashing rather than isolating cleanly.

Strong root-cause diagnoses: identifies [B,N,N,H] as uncoalesced (stride H=128) and switches to [B,H,N,N]; later identifies a 128x128 tile exceeds H100's 232KB shared memory. These distinguish a perf/hardware problem from a math/precision one (level-8 flavor).

Repeatedly states the SAME hypothesis — 'bottleneck is permute+contiguous copies, compute projections directly in [B,H,N,N]' — across many rewrites without ever resolving it; oscillates between bf16 (fast/inaccurate) and fp32 (accurate/slow). Classic non-convergence that pulls the score below the high anchors.

Distinguishes precision error (bf16 accumulation exceeding 2e-2) from perf and correctly refuses to sacrifice the correctness gate — reverts to exact fp32 Triton contraction. But this is partly a rationalized retreat: latency never met (52-238ms vs 10.4ms) and was ultimately abandoned rather than solved.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly clears level 5 (forms hypotheses, fixes specific causes like stride bugs and layout/shared-memory limits, re-verifies against a reference) and touches level 8 by explicitly distinguishing math-contract errors, bf16 precision errors, and perf/memory bottlenecks and making deliberate design changes (layout coalescing, fp32-projection/bf16-contraction splits). However it falls well short of level 10: it oscillates heavily between bf16 and fp32, restates the identical 'avoid permute copies' hypothesis six-plus times without converging, and never resolves the latency overshoot — ending by abandoning the budget rather than balancing the tension with a converging trade-off. This lands between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 6.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful latency measurement

evidence.note: Initial latency benchmark included clone/data-gen inside the timing loop (134ms N=2048); agent caught the pollution, showing measurement awareness but an ad-hoc starting point that did not yet mirror the grader.

Repeatedly 'benchmark all 10 shapes and compute max median latency' with 'proper warmup', consistently isolating N=2048 as the binding shape — matches grader's per-shape-median / max-over-10 structure and drives optimization toward the worst case.

Deliberately excluded data-generation from timing ('numbers inflated by including data generation'), a deviation from the grader which regenerates input each iteration; measured numbers stayed noisy and unreconciled (6.6ms isolated vs 40ms pipeline).

Explicitly rewrote bench_final.py 'to follow the spec exactly (regenerate input each iteration, reuse mask/weights/config)' with warmup and median — a grader-faithful harness, but only assembled at the very end; no explicit CUDA-event use and no variance/margin confirmation.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly used warmup, per-shape medians over all 10 shapes, and targeted the binding shape (N=2048), and by the end explicitly built a harness intended to reproduce the grader's regenerate-per-iteration/median/max protocol — squarely between the level-5 (CUDA-event+warmup+medians) and level-8 (full grader-faithful harness driving the binding shape) anchors. It falls short of a clean 8 because the fully grader-faithful harness only crystallized at the very end, earlier timing deviated from the grader (excluding data-gen) and produced noisy, unreconciled numbers, with no explicit CUDA-event timing or variance/margin accounting (level 10). This places observed behavior at 7.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon GPU-kernel task: implement AF3 outgoing TriMul as a Triton kernel that must be numerically correct across a large input domain (many B/N/dim combos, Normal and heavy-tailed Cauchy inputs, masked/unmasked) AND hit a hard latency budget (max of 10 per-shape medians ≤ 10400 μs on H100). Difficulty comes from a subtle math contract (outgoing contraction = left @ right.T over the inner axis, exact op ordering, mask placement, gate-before-final-linear), fp32 precision under a 2e-2 tolerance with heavy tails, tiling for N up to 2048, and the fact that the grader is not directly runnable — the agent must construct its own oracle. This warrants heavy, sustained meta-work: careful spec orientation, correctness-before-latency sequencing, a self-built verification oracle spanning the domain, and iterative adaptation to numerical/perf failures.

dimensions.name: Spec & environment orientation
dimensions.description: Extracting the exact TriMul contract from the spec (contraction direction, op ordering, mask placement, gate timing, shapes/tolerances) and probing the Triton/GPU environment before committing to an implementation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec has several easy-to-invert details (outgoing left@right.T vs left@right, mask applied once at the projection stage, LN_hidden then out_gate then to_out, nomask semantics). Misreading any one silently breaks correctness everywhere, so a correct mental model up front is the single highest-leverage investment.

anchors.0: Starts coding a kernel with no evidence of having parsed the contraction direction, op ordering, or shapes; treats the einsum as an ordinary matmul.
anchors.3: Reads the spec once and restates it loosely, but leaves ambiguous points (e.g. whether it's left@right or left@right.T, where the mask goes, gate-before-or-after to_out) unresolved before implementing.
anchors.5: Correctly identifies the core contract — outgoing contraction, mask-at-projection, LN→gate→to_out ordering, fp32, tolerance, hidden_dim=128 — and notes the target shape ranges before writing the kernel.
anchors.8: Distills a precise, itemized contract and cross-checks the subtle points against each other (e.g. confirms the einsum axis labels imply left@right.T, notes nomask==ones equivalence, flags Cauchy heavy tails + 2e-2 tolerance as a precision constraint) and probes Triton availability / GPU capabilities before design.
anchors.10: Builds a rigorous, self-consistent spec model AND anticipates the failure modes it implies (large-N tiling limits, fp32 accumulation of a K-sum over the sequence axis under heavy-tailed inputs, memory footprint at N=2048/dim=768), grounding early design choices in that analysis rather than discovering them later by trial.

dimensions.name: Correctness-first decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the build into ordered milestones — e.g. a plain reference implementation, a naive-but-correct Triton kernel, then optimization — each with an explicit done-check, rather than one monolithic push at a fused fast kernel.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec explicitly prioritizes correctness over latency. An agent that jumps straight to a fused, tiled, fast kernel conflates two hard problems and cannot localize bugs; staged milestones (correct math → correct Triton → fast Triton) make each failure diagnosable and protect the correctness gate.

anchors.0: No structure: one giant attempt at a fast fused kernel, correctness and performance entangled.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering only; may write a reference but doesn't use it as a milestone gate, or starts optimizing before any shape is verified correct.
anchors.5: Clear phases — reference PyTorch, then Triton correctness, then latency tuning — with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Explicit ordered milestones each with a concrete exit criterion (e.g. 'Triton matches reference within 2e-2 on all shapes' before touching perf), and sub-goals sequenced by risk (get the contraction/ordering right first, tile large N next, fuse last).
anchors.10: A milestone hierarchy that also sequences the domain deliberately (small shapes → large N → high dim → Cauchy/mask variants) and the latency budget by hardest shape, treating each as a checkpoint; the plan visibly governs execution order and is revisited as milestones complete.

dimensions.name: Self-built correctness oracle across the domain
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing an independent reference (e.g. a straightforward PyTorch/einsum TriMul) and comparing the kernel against it across the full supported domain and input distributions, since the actual grader cannot be run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader is hidden and correctness is the pass/fail priority under a tight 2e-2 tolerance. Without a self-built oracle exercised over B/N/dim variety, masked/unmasked, and Normal + Cauchy inputs, 'looks right' is worthless — verification IS the safety net for this task.

anchors.0: No independent check; correctness asserted from inspection or a single run with no reference.
anchors.3: Compares to a reference on one tiny shape / one distribution, or eyeballs a few numbers; no coverage of large N, high dim, mask, or Cauchy.
anchors.5: Builds a correct reference implementation and checks the kernel against it on several representative shapes with the specified tolerance, including at least one masked and one Cauchy case.
anchors.8: Systematic comparison harness sweeping the domain edges (N up to 2048, dim up to 768, B variants), both distributions, masked/unmasked and nomask, using rtol=atol=2e-2 as the gate; investigates any near-tolerance mismatch rather than accepting it.
anchors.10: Treats verification as an evolving instrument: parameterized sweeps over the full domain, targeted stress on the known-fragile cases (heavy-tailed Cauchy accumulation, largest shapes, mask edge behavior), reasons about worst-case numerical error vs the tolerance, and re-runs the full suite after every change so no optimization silently regresses correctness.

dimensions.name: Tracking correctness coverage and latency headroom
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which shapes/distributions are verified correct and where the latency stands against the 10400 μs budget, and detecting when debugging is going in circles.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Two moving targets (a wide correctness matrix and a max-over-10-shapes latency gate) are easy to lose track of; an agent that forgets which shapes still fail, or that keeps re-fixing the same numerical bug, will thrash away its horizon.

anchors.0: No sense of what's done vs remaining; repeats the same failed fix or declares success with large parts of the domain untested.
anchors.3: Vague tracking; conflates 'passed one shape' with 'passed', or loses track of which latency shape is the bottleneck.
anchors.5: Keeps a usable running account of which shapes/distributions pass and roughly where latency sits relative to budget.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit correctness-coverage picture and per-shape latency readout, identifies the binding (max) latency shape, and notices stalls/circular debugging and names them.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a done-vs-remaining ledger across both correctness and latency, catches regressions and thrash early, and reallocates effort to the actual bottleneck (worst shape or fragile distribution) rather than polishing already-passing cases.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on numerical & performance failures
dimensions.description: Revising design or approach when confronted with falsifying evidence — wrong contraction results, tolerance failures on Cauchy/large-N cases, tiling/memory limits, or latency overshoot — rather than pushing the same approach harder.
dimensions.why_it_matters: This task reliably produces divergence: heavy tails break naive accumulation, large N/dim breaks a single-tile kernel, and a correct-but-slow kernel misses the budget. Progress depends on diagnosing the true cause and changing the design, not brute-forcing.

anchors.0: Ignores failing checks or repeatedly retries the same broken kernel with cosmetic tweaks.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with trial-and-error patches lacking a diagnosis; may abandon correctness to chase speed or vice versa.
anchors.5: When a check fails, forms a plausible hypothesis, fixes the specific cause (e.g. accumulation dtype, tiling for large N, gate/mask placement) and re-verifies.
anchors.8: Diagnoses failures to root cause (distinguishes a math-contract error from a numerical-precision error from a perf problem) and makes deliberate design changes — e.g. re-tiling, changing accumulation strategy, restructuring the fused pass — validated against the oracle.
anchors.10: Systematically isolates each divergence, updates the design/plan in response, and balances the correctness/latency tension with principled trade-offs (never sacrificing the correctness gate for speed), demonstrating repeated evidence-driven pivots that converge rather than oscillate.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful latency measurement
dimensions.description: Building a timing methodology that mirrors the grader (CUDA-event timing, warmup discard, per-shape median, input regenerated per iteration, max over the 10 shapes) so latency decisions are based on trustworthy numbers.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The latency gate is precise and adversarial (max of 10 medians, specific timing protocol). Optimizing against a mismeasured proxy — no warmup, wall-clock timing, or the wrong shape — wastes effort and can hide a failing bottleneck shape, so how the agent measures is a genuine, separable meta-demand.

anchors.0: No latency measurement, or a single untimed run treated as 'fast enough'.
anchors.3: Ad hoc timing (wall clock, no warmup, one shape) that doesn't reflect the grader's protocol.
anchors.5: Uses CUDA-event timing with warmup on the relevant shapes and looks at medians rather than single samples.
anchors.8: Timing harness that reproduces the grader's methodology — warmup discard, per-shape median over repeated runs, input regenerated per iteration, evaluating the max across all 10 shapes — and uses it to target the binding shape.
anchors.10: A faithful, reusable benchmarking instrument that also accounts for measurement noise/variance, confirms the worst-case shape stays under budget with margin, and drives optimization decisions from these numbers rather than intuition, re-checking after each change.
